description_full: i3 Verticals, Inc. provides enterprise software and services solutions to public sector entities in the United States and Canada. The company offers digital solutions for dynamic processes to plan, coordinate, evaluate, record, and provide up to date information within court systems; E-Filing and revenue cycle management solutions for courts; solutions for computer aided dispatch, records management, evidence management, jail management, mobile solutions, and livescan; and software solutions for vehicle title and registration, driver's license and permit management, and motor carrier compliance for departments of transportation. It also provides digital customer engagement platform, comprising web, mobile, chat, and voice options; billing and back-office management software solutions and services; solutions for school lunch programs, including meal account management, point of sale, menu planning, nutritional analysis, food inventory and free, and reduced meal applications, as well as school event solutions, such as ticketing and concessions. In addition, the company offers government fund accounting software; digital land records solutions, including AI indexing of information; computer assisted mass appraisal solutions; licensing and permitting solutions that include automation every step of the application, renewal, and payment process; and tax and revenue collection management solutions. i3 Verticals, Inc. was founded in 2012 and is based in Nashville, Tennessee.

financial_summary: i3 Verticals, Inc. is a small-cap technology business with a $663M market cap on $213M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -12% over the past three years, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 1% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 85% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $4M in free cash flow — roughly 2 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.32×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage runs at 4.1×.

Management returns a meaningful 5.7% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 2.9% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.1× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 2% operating margin trails the Technology median (7%) by 5pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.

Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-25.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 49% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 37% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 45% and a beta of 0.86, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.47 vs 5y 0.79), so read it loosely.
About $6.3M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 61% in the 2020 crash and 37% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $2.13 (margin of safety -796%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 28%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $1.08 to $3.53 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: P/E 65.8 vs 26.7, EV/EBITDA 28.4 vs 16.4 and P/FCF 176.7 vs 25.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 34% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 0.6% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 0.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 4 covering analysts target $25.50 on average, 34% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 1% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.1%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.68).
It runs a 85% gross margin and converts 2% of revenue into free cash flow, or -7% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality is a concern: cash conversion of only 0.32x.
ROE of 5% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.6x equity multiplier).
It spends 8.6% of revenue on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $66.7M (10% of market cap).
Goodwill makes up 39% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -12.5% over 3 years and 7.3% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 37%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 0.6% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -29.0% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.1x depreciation (0.9% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 0, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 2.9%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 4 sales over the past year, net $257K bought.
It returns 5.7% a year to shareholders (5.7% in buybacks).
The share count has grown 10.0% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
Short interest is elevated at 48.3% of the float, 5.1 days to cover.
people: With about 1,202 employees, each generates about $177K of revenue, 0.5x the Technology median, and productivity has fallen 5.8% a year.
That works out to $3K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $351K (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
